quant.label: Quantitative history
quant.description: Uses serial evidence, linked records, statistics and explicit models to ask different historical questions. Labrousse’s prices, Henry’s reconstructed families, Benson’s voting groups, Thernstrom’s mobility and Curtin’s slave-trade estimates extend beyond cliometrics. Fogel’s counterfactuals and North’s institutions represent distinct economic programmes; Gutman’s criticism shows that evidence and interpretation remain contested within quantitative debate.

indigenous.label: Indigenous history & decolonizing methods
indigenous.description: Indigenous historical traditions, community knowledge and scholarly research meet in varied academic practices. Oral histories, family relationships, archival inquiry and collaborations contribute different resources; authority and methods remain situated.

See the distinct approaches for works, collaborators and evidence limits. Related scholarship includes Miller, White, Harris and Lutz; Stó:lō field-school practice credits community and university participants. Leddy’s 2010 reflection supplies a separately dated later case.

indigenous.scope_note: A selective grouping of independently rooted Indigenous historical practices and decolonizing research, with Andean, Haudenosaunee, Ojibwe, Cree, Métis, Wendat, Māori, Osage, Native Hawaiian, Yukon and Australian examples. Earlier writing, community knowledge, academic historical scholarship and decolonizing methodology have different histories. Community historians, academic historians and outside collaborators have different positions. Neither anthropology nor European theory is their common origin; no selection stands for every nation or protocol. Membership is a contextual intellectual contribution, not a binary Indigenous-identity classification. Journal counts are venue-based publication proxies and cannot date the origins of these practices or identify Indigenous authorship. Academic Indigenous history includes documented collaborations with scholars working across historical, anthropological and geographical inquiries. Shared research subjects do not establish intellectual descent. Later source dates are separate from earlier events; only Leddy’s 2010 article is accepted here as a selected post-2000 intervention.

cdn_national_tradition.label: Laurentian & national tradition
cdn_national_tradition.date_label: Staple studies 1923–40 · Creighton 1937 · Lower 1946 · Careless 1954 · Centenary Series volumes 1964–85 · Berger's analysis 1976
cdn_national_tradition.description: English-Canadian historical writing that took the transcontinental nation-state as its frame, from the interwar years to the centennial. Its economic core is the staple approach: Innis's studies of the fur trade (1930) and cod fisheries (1940) read Canada's development through exports to imperial centres, an approach Watkins later called Canada's most distinctive contribution to political economy. Creighton's Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence (1937) simplified and expanded Innis's thesis, making Montreal's merchants the 'spiritual fathers' of Confederation; his Macdonald biography followed. Liberal nationalists such as Lower and Underhill and conservative nationalists such as Creighton and Stacey disagreed politically while sharing the nation-state as the frame of reference. Careless offered a metropolitan interpretation (1954), which Donald Davis (1985) found indeterminate, and Morton asked in 1946 on what critical premises the established interpretations rested. The Canadian Centenary Series, from 1964, gathered national syntheses, including translated volumes by the Quebec historians Trudel and Ouellet. Cook's and Careless's 'limited identities' (1967, 1969) and the new regional history of Acadiensis (1971) challenged the frame, and Berger's Writing of Canadian History (1976) analysed the English-Canadian tradition as a historiographical subject. French-Canadian historians such as Michel Brunet pursued a rival national vision, treated under Quebec historiography.

Restatement: Watkins (1963). Analysis: Berger, The Writing of Canadian History (1976, 1986); Buckner (2000); Miville (2016). Critics: Cook (1967), Careless (1969), Buckner (1971), Davis (1985).
cdn_national_tradition.scope_note: A teaching umbrella, not one school. The staple approach (political economy), Creighton's Laurentian narrative, liberal and conservative nationalisms, metropolitanism and the Centenary Series are distinct projects; roster inclusion is not membership. The label avoids 'Laurentian school': no checked source uses that phrase. French-Canadian and Quebec national historiography belongs to Quebec historiography: Trudel and Ouellet are named only in the Centenary Series strand, and the Creighton–Brunet comparison is carried by the relationship note, not the roster. Stacey (official history, external policy) is placed in Canadian military history and Political, international & national history; Stanley appears as a secondary row for The Birth of Western Canada. Critics appear as critics.

liberal_order_framework.label: Liberal order framework
liberal_order_framework.date_label: State-formation roots: Curtis 1988, Greer and Radforth 1992 · McKay’s prospectus Dec. 2000 · debate volume 2009 · selected later readings
liberal_order_framework.description: A proposal to write Canadian history as the history of a liberal project of rule. Ian McKay's prospectus in the Canadian Historical Review (2000) offered a way past the impasse between socio-cultural and national-political history: map 'Canada' as the project through which liberal order (in Fecteau's paraphrase, an individualism of liberty, equality and property) became common sense in northern North America from the 1840s. Commentators identify Gramsci's hegemony and Fernande Roy's study of francophone business liberalism as its sources and link it to earlier state-formation research: Bruce Curtis on schooling and the census, and Allan Greer and Ian Radforth's Colonial Leviathan (1992). Constant and Ducharme's Liberalism and Hegemony (2009) tested it on rights, municipalities, conservation, families, women and racialized people, and First Nations. This entry reads the framework as closer to a history of capitalism than to moral regulation: its subject is how property, the individual and market relations became the terms of rule. In his 2009 reply McKay held that liberal order and capitalism cannot be conflated, yet after the 1840s could not easily be separated. Earlier social histories of seigneurial Quebec (Greer 1985) and Montreal's wage-earning families (Bradbury 1993) are read alongside it. Critics answered: Bryan Palmer argued that the framework sidesteps capitalism's changing structures. Jerry Bannister proposed a loyalist order before 1840. Ruth Sandwell found a-liberal families, and Nancy Christie faulted its neglect of religion and of women. Later histories of land, enclosure and taxation (Weaver, Greer, Heaman) carry its questions further.
liberal_order_framework.representative_figures_and_works: Roots: Curtis, Building the Educational State (1988), True Government by Choice Men? (1992), The Politics of Population (2001); Greer and Radforth, eds., Colonial Leviathan (1992). Prospectus: McKay, “The Liberal Order Framework” (CHR, 2000), drawing on Roy, Progrès, harmonie, liberté (1988). Debate: Sandwell (2003); Constant and Ducharme, eds., Liberalism and Hegemony (2009), with Bannister, Heaman, Curtis, Sandwell, Perry, Brownlie and McKay’s reply; the Underhill Review round table (Ajzenstat, Christie, Fecteau, Pâquet) and Palmer (2009). Liberty: Ducharme (2010), McNairn (2000). Transition to capitalism (read alongside): Greer, Peasant, Lord, and Merchant (1985); Bradbury, Working Families (1993). Property and capitalism: Weaver (2003), Greer (2012, 2018), Heaman (2017). Left history: McKay (2005, 2008).
liberal_order_framework.scope_note: A programme and its debate rather than a school: roster inclusion is not adoption. Curtis, Greer and Radforth wrote its roots before it was named; Christie, Palmer, Sandwell, Fecteau and Ajzenstat appear as critics; Bannister proposes a loyalist order for 1750–1840 (chapter title), its relation to McKay not characterized. Kept separate from moral regulation by the user (2026-10-12) as "a different project closer to history of capitalism"; that reading is editorial and is stated as such in the description. The overlap with histories of capitalism is noted in the description; it is not drawn as a link, because the fields have not connected (user, 2026-10-12). Greer (1985) and Bradbury (1993) are read alongside the framework, not as its roots or applications.

cdn_working_class.label: Canadian working-class history
cdn_working_class.date_label: Earlier institutional histories (Logan 1948) · Labour/Le Travailleur founded 1976 · Palmer 1979, Kealey 1980 · debate over culture 1981 · gender and family 1989–93 · selected later works
cdn_working_class.description: Canadian working-class history took shape in the 1970s as a new labour history of class, culture and community, set against an older institutional history of unions, labour politics and industrial relations (Logan 1948; Abella 1973; Bercuson 1974). The Canadian Committee on Labour History founded Labour/Le Travailleur in 1976. Palmer’s skilled workers in Hamilton (1979), Kealey’s Toronto workers (1980) and their history of the Knights of Labor (1982) were among its early monographs. In 1981 Kenneth McNaught framed the contrast as ‘E. P. Thompson vs Harold Logan’ and, by a later account, objected that social historians took a revolutionary goal as history’s purpose; Bercuson questioned working-class culture as an explanatory framework, and Kealey defended class analysis and culture. Social historians of poverty and the state widened the field: Copp’s Montreal working class (1974), Finkel on business and reform (1979), Struthers on unemployment (1983). Feminist historians remade it from within: Sangster on women on the left (1989), Parr’s gender of breadwinners (1990) and Bradbury’s working families (1993). Rouillard wrote the history of Quebec unionism in French (1989), and Heron’s Workers’ Revolt in Canada (1998) took the 1917–25 upheaval as a national subject. Palmer’s Descent into Discourse (1990) attacked the linguistic turn in social history. In 2000 Morton argued that the journal’s founding team had concealed a decade of stasis. Later work turned to deindustrialization (High 2003), the history of the left (McKay 2008) and Indigenous labour and the settler order.
cdn_working_class.representative_figures_and_works: Logan, Trade Unions in Canada (1948); Abella, Nationalism, Communism, and Canadian Labour (1973); Bercuson, Confrontation at Winnipeg (1974); Copp, The Anatomy of Poverty (1974); Labour/Le Travailleur (1976); Palmer, A Culture in Conflict (1979); Finkel, Business and Social Reform in the Thirties (1979); Kealey, Toronto Workers Respond to Industrial Capitalism (1980); McNaught, Bercuson and Kealey (1981); Kealey and Palmer, Dreaming of What Might Be (1982); Struthers, No Fault of Their Own (1983); Palmer, Working-Class Experience (1983; 1992); Heron, Working in Steel (1988); Rouillard, Histoire du syndicalisme au Québec (1989); Sangster, Dreams of Equality (1989); Palmer, Descent into Discourse (1990); Parr, The Gender of Breadwinners (1990); Lutz, “After the Fur Trade” (1992); Bradbury, Working Families (1993); Kealey, Workers and Canadian History (1995); Heron, The Workers’ Revolt in Canada (1998); Morton and Sangster in Labour/Le Travail 46 (2000). Later: High, Industrial Sunset (2003); McKay, Reasoning Otherwise (2008); Burrill (2019); Finkel on Palmer (2021).
cdn_working_class.scope_note: A national research field within labour history. The ‘old’ institutional history and the ‘new’ labour history are positions in a debate, not successive stages; Bercuson and McNaught are critics (their 1981 essays are now checked through Bercuson’s abstract and Finkel’s account of McNaught), and Morton’s 2000 critique comes from outside the new labour history. Marxist and Thompsonian resources are documented by McNaught’s title and Kealey’s defence of class analysis; no single theory is attributed to the field. Gender historians (Sangster, Parr, Bradbury) are treated mainly in Canadian women’s and gender history; they appear here for their working-class histories. Quebec labour history in French (Rouillard) is part of the field and of Quebec historiography. Poverty and welfare-state histories overlap with political history. Immigrant workers (Avery) are in the immigration entry; Indigenous labour is a strand, not a claim of adoption. Palmer’s Descent into Discourse (1990) is placed here as a critique of the linguistic turn, not as a critique of women’s history. McKay’s left history is a post-2000 contributor row; his main entry is Liberal order framework.

cdn_women_gender.label: Canadian women's & gender history
cdn_women_gender.date_label: Earlier women writers of history (recovered by Boutilier and Prentice 1997) and Cleverdon’s suffrage history 1950 · collections and studies 1976–79 · Collectif Clio 1982 · Prentice et al. 1988 · Parr 1990 · Left History exchange 1995–96 · selected publication milestones, not boundaries
cdn_women_gender.description: Canadian women's history studies women as historical actors in Canada and, increasingly from the 1990s, gender as a relation shaping work, family, politics, law and the state. Earlier women wrote national, local and regional history, recovered by Boutilier and Prentice (1997); Cleverdon studied the suffrage movement (1950); collections and studies of reform and women's organizations followed in the later 1970s (Cook and Mitchinson; Strong-Boag; Kealey). Two syntheses had different starting points. The Collectif Clio's L'histoire des femmes au Québec depuis quatre siècles (1982) rejected a male-centred history presented as everyone's history; Prentice and colleagues' Canadian Women: A History (1988) offered a collaborative survey. Studies of women and war (Pierson), women on the left (Sangster), working families in Montreal (Bradbury) and housewives in the Depression (Baillargeon) joined the field to labour and family history. Parr's comparison of two Ontario towns (1990) challenged assumptions about the separateness of gender and class roles. In the 1990s historians argued over whether gender history extended or displaced women's history: Pierson weighed the turn to deconstruction and Scott's theory of gender against experience and voice (1991), and Sangster's 'Beyond Dichotomies' (1995), by her later account, protested a hierarchy that set gender history above a 'limited' women's history; replies in Left History defended gender history (1996). Later work examined masculinity and gendered political languages (Morgan), sexuality and the law, and postwar domesticity and consumption (Parr, Korinek, Fahrni). Lévesque asked how far Quebec historiography had integrated women (1997); Quebec women's history is treated mainly under Quebec historiography.

strands.title: Earlier women writers of history
strands.focus: Women wrote Canadian history long before women’s history was a field: popular, local and regional historians (Machar, Skinner, Esther Clark Wright), the independent scholar Isabel Skelton, and a few university historians, among them Hilda Neatby and Margaret Ormsby, the CHA’s first and second women presidents (1962–63; 1965–66). In French Canada, Marie-Claire Daveluy wrote on New France. Most wrote national, local, fur-trade or political history; only Skelton (who “sought to write women back into Canadian history”, per Coulter’s reading of Crowley) and Daveluy (Bienvenue 2018) are documented as writing women in. They are earlier women writers of history, not founders of women’s history. Boutilier and Prentice’s Creating Historical Memory (1997) recovered this work and asked how professionalization masculinized history; the editors note that their subjects come mainly from “the white, Anglo-Celtic segment of society”. Cleverdon’s suffrage history (1950) is the earlier study of women that PhDs still cite. Bienvenue and Dorais (2023) extend the recovery to French Canada (after 2000).

cdn_immigration_ethnicity.label: Immigration, ethnicity & race in Canada
cdn_immigration_ethnicity.date_label: Ward 1978 · Avery 1979 · Abella and Troper 1982 · Perin 1983 · Anderson 1991 · Walker on race and the law 1997 · Backhouse 1999 · selected publication milestones, not boundaries
cdn_immigration_ethnicity.description: Studies immigration, ethnic communities, racism and the state in Canada: immigrant workers and their reception, ethnic identity, and the legal and spatial making of racial categories. The field expanded from the late 1970s. Ward's White Canada Forever (1978) traced west-coast prejudice against Asian residents and the discriminatory policies it produced; Avery's 'Dangerous Foreigners' (1979) examined European immigrant workers and labour radicalism; Abella and Troper studied Canada and the Jews of Europe, 1933–48 (1982). Perin's 'Clio as an Ethnic' (1983) asked whether ethnic groups had been 'discovered' just when the state faced challenges such as Quebec nationalism. Studies of Toronto neighbourhoods (Harney, who co-founded the Multicultural History Society of Ontario in 1976), Italian migrants in Montreal (Ramirez), Chinese Montrealers (Helly), Quebec's immigration policy (Pâquet 1997), British Columbia politicians (Roy), Italian immigrants in postwar Toronto (Iacovetta) and Ukrainian-Canadian women (Swyripa) followed. Anderson (1987, 1991) treated 'Chinese' and 'Chinatown' as racial categories made through government practice and place, which a reviewer saw as moving beyond earlier studies of white prejudice; Walker's Supreme Court case studies (1997) and Backhouse's Colour-Coded (1999) traced racism through law. Black Canadian history, including Black migration and immigration control, is a separate entry. Post-2000 work turned to Cold War reception and citizenship (Iacovetta 2006; Bohaker and Iacovetta 2009).

native_newcomer.label: Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history
native_newcomer.date_label: Earlier resources: Innis 1930, Stanley 1936 · Ray 1974 · Van Kirk and Brown 1980 · Trigger’s Natives and Newcomers 1985 · Miller 1989 · Milloy 1999 · selected later works
native_newcomer.description: A Canadian historiography of relations between Indigenous peoples and European newcomers, centred first on the fur trade and then on policy, schools, missions, health and labour. Innis’s Fur Trade in Canada (1930) was subtitled ‘an introduction to Canadian economic history’. From the 1970s historians, geographers and archaeologists recast it with Indigenous people as actors: trappers, hunters and middlemen (Ray 1974), wives and kin in fur-trade society (Van Kirk; Brown, both 1980), and Wendat history across contact (Trigger 1976, 1985; Delâge 1985), while Dickason studied European representations of them (1984). The field long called itself ‘native–newcomer’ history, after Trigger’s Natives and Newcomers (1985); current usage prefers ‘Indigenous’. Miller (1989) offered a national synthesis of ‘Indian–white relations’. Later work studied reserve farming and policy (Carter 1990), residential schools (Miller 1996; Milloy 1999), health (Kelm 1998) and wage labour (Lutz 1992). Brownlie and Kelm (1994) asked whether agency-centred work on Indian policy and the potlatch law (Cole and Chaikin; Miller; Loo) had made Native agency a colonialist alibi. Indigenous scholars questioned the framing: Sioui (1989) found conventional history without a method for Indigenous self-interpretation; Winona Stevenson (Wheeler) (1998) argued that historians of ‘Indian–White relations’, relying on one side’s records, kept even agency-centred work within a colonialist framework and set oral history aside; LaRocque (1999) found that the cross-cultural ethnohistory of Trigger, Brown and Van Kirk still ‘othered’ its subjects. After 2000, settler-colonial analysis read this history as continuing dispossession; Greer replied that the fur trade’s commercial penetration was a different form of invasion.

Later: Rutherdale (2002), Brownlie (2003), Raibmon (2005), Podruchny (2006), Lutz, Makúk (2008). Critics and alternatives: Sioui (1989), Paul, We Were Not the Savages (1993; 2000 edition), Stevenson [Wheeler], “The Othering of Indigenous History” (1998), LaRocque (1999); in the US, Fixico (2009) and S. A. Miller (2009).
native_newcomer.scope_note: A research field in mostly academic, mostly non-Indigenous Canadian historiography, built on company, church and state archives together with archaeology and anthropology. It is not the atlas’s Indigenous history entry, which centres Indigenous historical traditions, community knowledge and authority. Several people sit in both (Dickason, Miller, Lutz, Trigger); their existing contexts are kept, and Indigenous historical practice is not subsumed here. It is not Settler colonialism, which reads dispossession as a continuing structure: most works here predate that framework, and whether any adopts it was not checked; and Greer’s critique points the other way. Indigenous critiques of the ‘relations’ framing (Sioui, LaRocque; Fixico and S. Miller in the US) appear as critics, not members, and the roster records no identity classification. Francophone work is thin in this selection (Delâge, Sioui); New France encounter history overlaps with Quebec historiography. The label keeps the field’s word ‘newcomer’ but uses ‘Indigenous’; ‘native–newcomer’, Trigger’s 1985 term, is explained in the description as the field’s historical name. ‘Indigenous–settler’ is avoided so as not to collide with Settler colonialism.

strands.focus: Trigger joins archaeology and documents to Wendat/Huron history before and after contact (1976) and reconsiders the ‘heroic age’ of New France (1985). Delâge writes the same encounter in French (1985); Dickason studies European representations (1984). Shared with the Ethnohistory entry.

strands.title: How historians wrote about Indigenous peoples
strands.focus: Walker (1971) and Trigger (1986) survey Canadian historical writing about Indigenous peoples. Trigger dates such studies from 1971 and describes ethnohistorical work across disciplines moving into national history.
strands.works: Walker, “The Indian in Canadian Historical Writing” (1971); Trigger, “The Historians’ Indian” (1986)

strands.title: Syntheses of relations and policy
strands.focus: Miller’s national synthesis of ‘Indian–white relations’ (1989), Dickason’s history of First Nations (1992), and regional or biographical studies (Smith 1987; Coates 1991). Miller’s and Dickason’s books differ in authorship and standpoint; they are grouped here as syntheses, not as one interpretation.
strands.works: Smith, Sacred Feathers (1987); Miller, Skyscrapers Hide the Heavens (1989); Coates, Best Left as Indians (1991); Dickason, Canada’s First Nations (1992)

strands.title: Reserves, residential schools and Indian agents
strands.focus: Reserve agriculture and policy (Carter 1990), residential schools (Miller 1996; Milloy 1999) and Indian agents (Brownlie 2003). Most predate the settler-colonial framework; whether any adopts it was not checked.
strands.works: Carter, Lost Harvests (1990); Miller, Shingwauk’s Vision (1996); Milloy, “A National Crime” (1999); Brownlie, A Fatherly Eye (2003)

strands.title: Health, missions and authenticity
strands.focus: Kelm reads health and healing through the body and colonial power (1998); Rutherdale studies gender and race in the mission field (2002); Raibmon treats authenticity as made by unequal collaborators (2005).
strands.works: Kelm, Colonizing Bodies (1998); Rutherdale, Women and the White Man’s God (2002); Raibmon, Authentic Indians (2005)

strands.title: Indigenous labour after the fur trade
strands.focus: Lutz treats Aboriginal people in British Columbia as a labouring class (1992) and later rewrites Aboriginal–white relations (2008). This is the strand that meets Canadian working-class history.
strands.works: Lutz, “After the Fur Trade” (1992); Makúk (2008)

strands.title: Agency as alibi? An internal critique
strands.focus: Brownlie and Kelm (1994) criticised agency-centred work on Indian policy and the potlatch law (Cole and Chaikin 1990; Miller; Loo 1992): stressing Native agency exaggerated how far it became effective self-defence, trivialising the harm of colonial policy and serving as an ‘alibi’ for it. A critique within policy history, not of the fur-trade literature; targets known from a secondary source, essay unread.
strands.works: Robin Brownlie and Mary-Ellen Kelm, “Desperately Seeking Absolution: Native Agency as Colonialist Alibi?” CHR 75:4 (December 1994): 543–56

strands.title: Indigenous critiques of the relations frame
strands.focus: Sioui (1989), Stevenson/Wheeler (1998) and LaRocque (1999) criticise the relations framing from Indigenous standpoints: its reliance on colonial documents, its disregard of oral history and its ethnological distance. Fixico and S. Miller (2009, US) question ‘Indian–white relations’ as the premise of Indian history. Paul’s We Were Not the Savages (1993; the 2000 Fernwood edition is the one PhDs cite), subtitled ‘a Mi’kmaq perspective’, rejects the ‘savage’ category (title and subtitle only). Adams’s Prison of Grass (1975) is an earlier counter-history of official history, not a critique of this field, and Dickason is a member of the field. Trigger (1986) and Brownlie and Kelm (1994) are non-Indigenous critiques from inside. These are critics and alternatives, not members.
strands.works: Sioui (1989); Paul (1993; 2000 ed.); Stevenson [Wheeler] (Fall 1998); LaRocque (1999); Fixico (2009); S. A. Miller (2009)

strands.title: After 2000: the settler-colonial reading and its critics
strands.focus: Settler-colonial analysis reads reserves, schools and dispossession as a continuing structure. Greer replies that the settler mode dominates some periods and regions and fades in others, and that commercial penetration (the fur trade’s mode) and extractivism are other forms of invasion. Konishi records Indigenous scholars’ critiques of settler colonial studies. Later readings only.
strands.works: Greer, “Settler Colonialism and Beyond” (JCHA 2019); Konishi (2019)

quebec_historiography.label: Quebec historiography
quebec_historiography.date_label: Earlier national history (Groulx) · Institut d’histoire de l’Amérique française founded 1946, its Revue from 1947 · Montreal and Laval schools 1950s–60s · Histoire du Québec contemporain 1979 · Rudin’s critique 1992 · selected later readings (Catholic Action revision 2002–05)
quebec_historiography.description: Historical writing on Quebec and French Canada, mostly in French, long organized around the nation, the Conquest of 1760 and the meaning of modernity. Lionel Groulx’s national history of French Canada closes what a francophone anthology calls the time of the ‘ancients’; Groulx founded the Institut d’histoire de l’Amérique française (1946) and its Revue (1947). In the 1950s historians at Montréal (Séguin, Frégault, Brunet) made the Conquest and its consequences their central problem. At Laval, Trudel wrote the history of New France, and Hamelin and Ouellet economic and social history, Ouellet in a conjunctural idiom indebted to Labrousse. Their agricultural-crisis thesis (1962) was contested by Paquet and Wallot (1972–73); Dechêne, trained in the Annales milieu in France, wrote the social history of seventeenth-century Montreal (1974). After 1970 a modernist generation turned to contemporary, urban and industrial Quebec and to its whole population (Linteau, Durocher and Robert, 1979). Women’s history followed, from the Collectif Clio (1982) to Baillargeon (1991); Lévesque (1997) asked how far colleagues had integrated it. Behiels (1985) found the Quiet Revolution’s prelude in 1945–60; Rouillard (1997) recorded a shift from reading it as rupture to turn. Ronald Rudin (1992, 1997) argued that the modernists’ search for a ‘normal’ society muted religion, rurality and ethnicity; Linteau and Fecteau replied (1995). Bouchard and Lamonde (2000) close the period; after 2000, Meunier and Warren, Bienvenue and Gauvreau traced the Quiet Revolution to Catholic Action.
quebec_historiography.representative_figures_and_works: Groulx, Histoire du Canada français depuis la découverte (1950); IHAF (1946) and RHAF (1947); Séguin, La “nation canadienne” et l’agriculture (thesis 1947; 1970); Frégault, La guerre de la Conquête (1955); Brunet, La présence anglaise et les Canadiens (1958); Trudel, L’esclavage au Canada français (1960) and Histoire de la Nouvelle-France (1963–); Hamelin, Économie et société en Nouvelle-France (1960); Ouellet and Hamelin, “La crise agricole dans le Bas-Canada” (1962); Ouellet, Histoire économique et sociale du Québec, 1760–1850 (1966); Paquet and Wallot (1972–73); Wallot, Un Québec qui bougeait (1973); Dechêne, Habitants et marchands (1974); Savard (1974); Gagnon, Le Québec et ses historiens (1978); Linteau, Durocher and Robert, Histoire du Québec contemporain (1979; 1986); Collectif Clio (1982); Linteau, “La nouvelle histoire du Québec vue de l’intérieur” (1983); Behiels, Prelude to Quebec’s Quiet Revolution (1985); Lévesque, La norme et les déviantes (1989) and “Réflexions sur l’histoire des femmes dans l’histoire du Québec” (1997); Baillargeon, Ménagères au temps de la Crise (1991); Rudin, “Revisionism and the Search for a Normal Society” (1992; French 1995) and Making History in Twentieth-Century Quebec (1997); Linteau and Fecteau (1995); Dumont, Genèse de la société québécoise (1993); Dickinson and Young, A Short History of Quebec (1993 ed.); Bouchard (1996, 2000); Martel (1997); Rouillard, “La Révolution tranquille: rupture ou tournant?” (1997); Lamonde (2000). Later: Meunier and Warren, Sortir de la « grande noirceur » (2002); Bienvenue, Quand la jeunesse entre en scène (2003); Gauvreau, The Catholic Origins of Quebec’s Quiet Revolution (2005); Bédard and Goyette, eds., Parole d’historiens (2006); Baillargeon, Brève histoire des femmes au Québec (2012).
quebec_historiography.scope_note: A research field defined by its object (Quebec and French Canada) and largely by its language. The Montreal school, Laval, the modernists and their critics are distinct and overlapping positions, not one school; Savard warns against treating ‘École de Québec’ as a unit. The post-1970 generation is called ‘modernist’ after Bédard and Goyette’s part title; Linteau calls it a ‘nouvelle histoire’; Rudin’s polemical name for it is used only in the normal-society debate strand. Annales influence is indirect and contested: Ouellet’s Labroussian economic history, Mandrou’s preface and Dechêne’s training in the Annales milieu are documented, while Linteau says his generation owed more to sociology and American historians. Groulx’s nationalism and clerical politics are historical subjects here, not the atlas’s categories. Quebec women’s history (Clio, Lévesque, Baillargeon) and the Catholic Action revision of the Quiet Revolution have their primary homes here. English-language historians of Quebec (Behiels, Dickinson, Young, Rudin, Greer) belong to the field. Acadian and francophone-minority historiography outside Quebec is only touched by Martel. New France encounter history with Indigenous peoples is in Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history.

strands.focus: Groulx’s national history and his conception of history. Groulx founded the Institut d’histoire de l’Amérique française in 1946 and its Revue in 1947, and wrote in its first issue. The anthology places him at the end of ‘le temps des Anciens’.

strands.title: The Montreal school and the Conquest
strands.focus: Séguin, Frégault and Brunet make the Conquest and its economic and national consequences their central problem; Savard groups them by shared ideological outlook. Ouellet (1985) calls Séguin the ‘théoricien de l’École néo-nationaliste’, for whom the Conquest decapitated the national bourgeoisie, a thesis Brunet took up in the 1950s; Tousignant (1980) calls Séguin the school’s ‘maître à penser’ and describes the gulf between it and Ouellet.

strands.title: Laval: economic and social history
strands.focus: Trudel’s history of New France and of slavery in French Canada; Hamelin and Ouellet’s economic and social history of New France and Lower Canada. strands.title: The Lower Canadian agricultural crisis debate
strands.focus: Ouellet and Hamelin’s 1962 thesis that a fall in wheat production from 1802, with population pressure and peasant routine, lay behind French-Canadian nationalism and, ‘en grande partie’, the rebellion of 1837–38; Paquet and Wallot’s 1972 rejection of it as ‘irrecevable’ and their market-rational habitant, with Wallot’s Quebec ‘qui bougeait’; Ouellet’s reply (1976), defending the production-based explanation and disputing his critics’ reading of his argument; Le Goff’s review of the controversy (1974, unread); Tousignant’s critique of Le Bas-Canada (1980); and Greer’s rejection of the ‘atavistic mentality’ explanation (1981). Ouellet (1985) names later entrants (Isbester, McCallum, McInnis, Courville). The 1962, 1972, 1976 and 1980 texts and Greer (1981) were read for the Ouellet person entry. The exchange is not presented as resolving the crisis’s chronology, causes or explanatory reach; Paquet and Wallot themselves doubted the debate was settled.
strands.works: Ouellet and Hamelin (1962); Ouellet (1966, 1976); Paquet and Wallot (1972, 1973); Wallot (1973); Le Goff (1974); Tousignant (1980); Greer (1981)

strands.title: New France as social history
strands.focus: Dechêne’s habitants and merchants of seventeenth-century Montreal, from a Paris doctorate (1973) after training in the Annales milieu of Mandrou and Goubert; Hamelin’s economy and society of New France.
strands.works: Dechêne (1974); Hamelin (1960)

strands.title: The modernist synthesis
strands.focus: Linteau describes his generation’s turn to c. 1850–present, to urban and industrial Quebec, and to the history of Quebec’s whole population rather than French Canadians alone; social history and serial sources, with Annales influence filtered through sociology and American history. Histoire du Québec contemporain and Dickinson and Young’s Short History are its syntheses.
strands.works: Linteau, Durocher and Robert (1979; 1986); Linteau (1983); Dickinson and Young (1993 ed.)

strands.title: Quebec women’s history
strands.focus: Collectif Clio’s four-century history (1982), Lévesque’s norms and “deviant” women (1989), Baillargeon’s Depression housewives (1991) and her short synthesis (2012). Lévesque (1997) judged that women’s history had redefined traditional Quebec history while some colleagues were slow to integrate women. The anthology places Clio and Micheline Dumont in its modernist part. Primary here: 31 of 34 PhDs citing this literature engage Quebec historiography; Canadian women's & gender history keeps its critique edge (edge_841). The Collectif Clio (1982) was Micheline Dumont, Michèle Jean, Marie Lavigne and Jennifer Stoddart; shared methods or positions are not inferred.
strands.works: Collectif Clio (1982); Lévesque (1989, 1997); Baillargeon (1991, 2012)

strands.title: Origins of the Quiet Revolution: rupture or turn?
strands.focus: Behiels finds the Quiet Revolution’s prelude in 1945–60 liberal and neo-nationalist debate (1985); Rouillard records historians’ shift from ‘rupture’ to ‘tournant’ (1997). The Catholic Action strand extends the argument after 2000.
strands.works: Behiels (1985); Rouillard, “La Révolution tranquille: rupture ou tournant?” (1997)

strands.title: Catholic Action and the Quiet Revolution
strands.focus: Against the Quiet Revolution’s own story of a clerical “grande noirceur”, Catholic Action, personalism and lay movements from the 1930s are read as preparing the 1960s. Two versions (Baum): social democracy (Meunier and Warren) and the family and gender (Gauvreau). Gauvreau judged that Quebec religious history had repeated the Quiet Revolution’s own ideology until these studies. strands.title: The ‘normal society’ debate
strands.focus: Rudin argues that the revisionists’ normal, Western Quebec muted religion, rurality and ethnicity (1992; 1995; 1997). Linteau and Fecteau reply in the Bulletin d’histoire politique (1995), and Fecteau reviews Rudin’s book on nationhood and the “revisionist school” (CHR 1999). strands.focus: Savard’s quarter-century survey (1974), Serge Gagnon on Quebec historians from Garneau to Groulx (1978), Rudin (1997), and Bédard and Goyette’s anthology (2006), whose four parts give a francophone periodization.

strands.focus: Dumont’s genesis of Quebec society (1993), Bouchard’s Saguenay and comparative New World nations (1996, 2000), Lamonde’s social history of ideas (2000) and Martel on the end of a pan-Canadian French Canada (1997).

cdn_political_national.label: Political, international & national history
cdn_political_national.date_label: Granatstein 1975, 1977, 1982 · Whitaker 1977 · Stacey 1977–81 · Bothwell, Drummond and English 1981 · Owram 1986 · Buckner 1993 · Whitaker and Marcuse 1994 · British World 2006 · CHA political history prizes first listed 2011 · Heaman's 'new political history' 2017 · selected later works
cdn_political_national.description: Research on the Canadian state, its parties, officials, wars and foreign relations, and the national syntheses built from them. Granatstein's histories of the King government at war (1975), of conscription (with Hitsman, 1977) and of the Ottawa mandarins (1982), Whitaker's study of the Liberal party and the state (1977) and Owram's history of the intellectuals who argued for planning and reform (1986) examined how federal power was organized, staffed and justified. Stacey's history of external policies (1977, 1981), Hillmer and Granatstein's Empire to Umpire (1994) and Bothwell's Alliance and Illusion (2007) treated Canada's place in the world. Bothwell, Drummond and English's Canada since 1945 (1981) and Thompson and Seager's Centenary Series volume (1985) offered national syntheses; political biography (Brown on Borden, Bélanger on Laurier, English on Pearson) and Bliss's business history kept leaders and enterprise in view. Whitaker and Marcuse's Cold War Canada (1994) turned to the security state. Buckner's 1993 address, asking historians to restore the settlement colonies to imperial history, led to the British World volume (2006). Chapnick (2000, 2005) questioned the middle-power 'golden age'. Granatstein and Bliss also led the national side of the 'Who Killed Canadian History?' debate. Since 2011 the CHA's political history prizes have rewarded a 'new political history' of state, tax and governance: Heaman on taxation (2017), Loo on forced relocation (2019), Bohaker on Anishinaabe governance (2020), and francophone studies of Hydro-Québec (Savard) and cultural policy (Harvey) that are recognized but not yet widely cited.

cdn_regional.label: Canadian regional history
cdn_regional.date_label: Morton's Manitoba 1957 · Ormsby's British Columbia 1958 · Craig's Upper Canada 1963 · 'limited identities' 1967–69 · Acadiensis 1971 · Acheson 1972 · Forbes 1979 · Friesen 1984 · Barman 1991 · reassessments 2000
cdn_regional.description: Histories of Canada's regions as places with their own economies, societies and identities rather than as peripheries of a central-Canadian story. Provincial syntheses such as Morton's Manitoba (1957) and Ormsby's British Columbia (1958) preceded the 'limited identities' argument: Cook (1967) suggested that Canadianism might be found in regional, ethnic and class identities, and Careless (1969) made the phrase a programme. Acadiensis was revived in 1971 (Windsor's initiative; Buckner editor), its first editorial faulting historians 'obsessed with the great "national" themes'. Acheson (1972) traced Maritime industrial growth under the National Policy and its subordination to Montreal capital, and Forbes studied the Maritime Rights movement (1979). Friesen (1984), Barman (1991), Conrad and Hiller (2001) and Waiser (2005) wrote regional syntheses, while Owram, Carter and Harris tied western and Pacific history to expansionist ideas, reserve policy and colonial geography. Ontario had provincial histories of its own (Craig 1963; Nelles 1974; McCalla 1993). Acadia became a growing Atlantic literature: Griffiths on Acadian history and identity (1992, 2005), Plank and Faragher on conquest and expulsion (2001, 2005), and Reid, Basque and colleagues on 1710 (2004). Francophone regional history worked at other scales: Painchaud on the Church and French Prairie settlement (a 1970s study, published posthumously in 1987), Landry and Lang's Histoire de l'Acadie (2001), and Quebec's intraprovincial regional histories, which Harvey contrasts with interprovincial regionalism. By 2000 McKay asked whether 'region' could hold the new histories of gender, ethnicity and community, and Buckner revisited limited identities.

Critique: McKay, "A Note on 'Region'" (2000).
cdn_regional.scope_note: A research field for Canada's regions (the Prairie West, British Columbia, the Atlantic provinces including Acadia, and Ontario) and the limited-identities argument. Provincial syntheses, regional economic history, rural history and regional identity are distinct strands. Indigenous and settler-colonial histories of the West and British Columbia overlap strongly (Carter, Harris) and are primarily placed in Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history, Settler colonialism and environment. Ontario has a strand of provincial syntheses and economic histories chosen by PhD citation counts; Acadia has its own Atlantic strand. The North and Newfoundland are small in the PhD corpus (about 18 and 9 titles) and get only this note. Quebec's regional history appears only as a contrast of scale. Roster inclusion does not imply that historians accepted "limited identities".

strands.title: Acadia (Atlantic)
strands.focus: Acadia before and after the expulsion of 1755. In the PhD corpus this is a substantial and rising literature: 101 of 1,303 PhDs (2009–2026) cite Acadian history works, 5.1% in 2009–14 and 8.9% in 2020–26, 23 of them at francophone universities. Griffiths, an authority on pre-1755 Acadia, wrote on its contexts to 1784 (1992) and the emergence of Acadian identity (2005); Plank (2001) and Faragher (2005) studied the British campaign against the peoples of Acadia and the expulsion; Reid, Basque and colleagues read the 1710 conquest from imperial, Acadian and Mi'kmaw perspectives (2004). settler_colonialism.label: Settler colonialism
settler_colonialism.date_label: Earlier settler-society studies 1983–95 · Wolfe 1999 · selected later readings: Wolfe 2006, Veracini 2010, journal 2011, critiques 2013–20; field chronology unresolved
settler_colonialism.description: Historical inquiry into colonial formations in which newcomers came to stay, acquired land and claimed sovereignty over Indigenous territories. Patrick Wolfe's account of settler colonialism as a structure rather than an event treats invasion as a continuing relation rather than a completed frontier past. Lorenzo Veracini's work and the journal Settler Colonial Studies (2011) distinguished settler colonial from colonial phenomena. Comparative studies of settler capitalism and settler societies, and decolonization-era uses of the term, came earlier. In Canadian historical writing the framework meets an older historiography of dispossession, reserves, gender and the state in the West and British Columbia. It also meets Indigenous political theory of recognition, sovereignty and resurgence. Its uses extend to labour, science, memory and settler identity. The field is contested from several directions. Indigenous scholars ask whether it recentres settlers and displaces Indigenous studies and Indigenous-authored histories. Historians question its structural inevitability and its fit across regions and periods, proposing other modes such as commercial penetration and extractivism. Black studies scholars question how it places slavery. Settler colonialism overlaps with Indigenous history, postcolonial critique and historical geography without being equivalent to any of them.
settler_colonialism.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier: Denoon, Settler Capitalism (1983); Stasiulis and Yuval-Davis, eds., Unsettling Settler Societies (1995). Wolfe, Settler Colonialism and the Transformation of Anthropology (1999) and “Settler Colonialism and the Elimination of the Native” (2006); Elkins and Pedersen, eds. (2005); Veracini, Settler Colonialism (2010) and Settler Colonial Studies (2011). Read with Coulthard (2014), A. Simpson (2014), L. B. Simpson (2011, 2017), Byrd (2011) and Tuck and Yang (2012). Canadian historiography: Carter (1990, 2008), Harris (2002, 2004, 2020), Perry (2001), Regan (2010), Daschuk (2013), Battell Lowman and Barker (2015), Burrill (2019). Critiques: Macoun and Strakosch (2013), Rowse (2014), Kauanui (2016), Greer (2019), Shoemaker (2019), Konishi (2019), Garba and Sorentino (2020).
settler_colonialism.scope_note: A selective research field whose theoretical consolidation came mostly after 2000; the entry covers its roots through 2000 and cites selected later works as readings. Settler-colonial theory, Indigenous political thought, Canadian histories of dispossession and comparative imperial history have different genealogies. Roster inclusion is not adoption of the paradigm: Carter, Perry, Harris and Daschuk wrote earlier or beside it. No single founder, origin or Canadian consensus is asserted. Critics appear as critics. Francophone uptake in the PhD corpus is near zero.
